procedural_history.originating_court: Kerala University (disciplinary action initiated by the Vice-Chancellor)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the Vice-Chancellor (approved by the Syndicate of the University) debarring the appellant from appearing in any examination for a year.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant challenged the Vice-Chancellor's order by a writ petition under Article 226 in the Kerala High Court. A Single Judge of the High Court allowed the petition and set aside the Vice-Chancellor's order. However, a Division Bench of the High Court reversed the Single Judge's decision in appeal.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the decision of the Division Bench of the Kerala High Court.

decision.appeal_result: The appeal fails and is dismissed with costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court, in its jurisdiction under Article 226, is justified in interfering with the decisions of domestic tribunals appointed by educational bodies, such as universities, in cases of unfair means.

law.fact: Domestic tribunals set up by educational bodies, like universities, have the jurisdiction to decide on cases of unfair means by students.
law.text: Universities or appellant No. I set up Enquiry Commit· tees to deal with the problem posed by the adoption of unfair means by candidates, and normally it is within the jurisdiction of such domestic tribunals lo decide all relevant questions in the light of the evidence 'tdduccd before them.

law.fact: The High Court's power under Article 226 is a limited jurisdiction for judicial review, not an appeal over the tribunal's decision.
law.text: Jn dealing with the validity of the impugned orders passed by Universities under Art. 226, the High Court is not sitting in a appeal over the decision in question: its jurisdiction is limited

law.fact: These domestic inquiries must be fair, follow the rules of natural justice, and give students an adequate opportunity to defend themselves.
law.text: Enquiries held by domestic Tribunals in such cases must, no doubt, be fair and students against whom char.ges are framed must be given adequate opportunities to defend themselves, and in holding such enquiries, the Tribunal. must scrupulously follow rules of natural justice;

law.fact: The strict rules and standards of evidence from criminal trials do not apply to these domestic inquiries; they can rely on probabilities and circumstantial evidence.
law.text: direct evidence may sometimes be available, but cases may arise where direct evidence is not available and !he question will have lo be considered in the light of probabilities and circumstantial evidence. ... it would, we think, not be reasonable to import into these enquiries all con-siderations which l!OVern criminal trials in ordinary courts of law.

application.fact: The Supreme Court held that courts should be slow to interfere with the decisions of these educational tribunals unless there is a clear justification.
application.text: This pro- blem which educational institutions have to face from time to time is a serious problem and unless there is justi- fication to do so, courts should be slow to interfere with the decisions of domestic Tribunals appointed by educa· tional bodies like the Universities.

application.fact: A High Court is only justified in quashing a tribunal's order if it is supported by no evidence at all.
application.text: if the impugned order is not supported by any evidence at all, the High Court would be justified to quash that order.

application.fact: When determining if there is "no evidence," the High Court must consider whether probabilities and circumstantial evidence could justify the tribunal's conclusion.
application.text: But the conclusion that the impugned order is not supported by any evidence must be reached after considering the question as to whe· ther probabilities and circumstantial evidence do not justify the said conclusion.

application.fact: In the present case, the Court found the university's inquiry was fair, the student had a chance to defend himself, and there was no allegation of bias, so there was no justification for the High Court to interfere.
application.text: Jn the present case, no animus is sugges- ted and no ma/a (ides have been pleaded. TI1e enquiry has been fair and the respondent has had an opportunity of making his defence. That hein~ so. we think the High Court was not justified in interfering with the order passed against the respondent.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that a High Court is not justified in interfering with the decisions of an educational body's domestic tribunal under Article 226, as long as the tribunal's inquiry is fair, follows the principles of natural justice, and its decision is supported by some evidence, which can include probabilities and circumstantial evidence. The High Court's role is not to re-evaluate the evidence as an appellate court but only to intervene if the decision is based on no evidence whatsoever or if the procedure was unfair.

issue.issue_text: Whether the principles of natural justice were violated because the appellant was not furnished with a copy of the inquiry officer's report before being called upon to give his explanation.

facts: The appellant was not provided with a copy of the inquiry officer's report before he was asked to submit his explanation in response to a show-cause notice.
The appellant was informed of the charge against him, the inquiry was held in his presence, he was allowed to cross-examine witnesses, and he was permitted to present his own evidence.
The appellant did not ask for a copy of the report at the time.
The inquiry officer was an impartial person.
law: The rules of natural justice are not embodied or rigid rules.
The requirements of natural justice depend on the facts and circumstances of the case, the constitution of the tribunal, and the rules under which it functions.
The core requirements of natural justice are that the accused person knows the nature of the accusation, is given an opportunity to state their case, and the tribunal acts in good faith.
There was no statutory or other rule that required the Vice-Chancellor to provide the appellant with a copy of the inquiry officer's report.
application: The Court determined that the fundamental requirements of natural justice had been met because the appellant was fully aware of the charge and was given a fair opportunity to defend himself during the inquiry.
The Court noted that there was no specific rule obligating the authorities to provide the report.

The Court emphasized that the appellant never requested a copy of the report. It reasoned that if he had felt it was necessary for his explanation, he could have asked for it. The Court viewed his subsequent complaint on this point as an "after thought."
Therefore, the Court found that the overall procedure was fair and just, and the failure to proactively provide the report did not constitute a violation of natural justice in these circumstances.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's contention, holding that there was no breach of the principles of natural justice. The Court reasoned that the appellant had received a fair inquiry, was aware of the charges, had the opportunity to defend himself, and had never requested a copy of the report, which no rule required to be furnished to him.

issue.issue_text: Whether the inquiry held against the appellant for adopting unfair means was fair and provided adequate opportunities for defence.

facts: An inquiry was initiated against the appellant for alleged malpractice during an examination.
The Vice-Chancellor appointed an Inquiry Officer, who submitted a report finding the appellant guilty.
Based on this report, the appellant was issued a show-cause notice and was subsequently debarred for a year after his explanation was found unsatisfactory.
The appellant contended the inquiry was unfair, primarily because he was not given a copy of the Inquiry Officer's report before he was required to submit his explanation.
law: Inquiries held by domestic tribunals, such as university committees, must be fair and provide the accused with adequate opportunities to defend themselves.
The principles of natural justice must be followed, which require that the accused knows the charge, is given an opportunity to state their case, and that the tribunal acts in good faith.
However, these inquiries are not expected to follow all the strict procedural considerations of a criminal trial.
The requirements of natural justice are not rigid or embodied in a fixed set of rules; their application depends on the specific facts and circumstances of each case.
application: The Court determined that the core elements of a fair inquiry were present: the appellant was informed of the charge against him, the inquiry was held in his presence, he was allowed to cross-examine witnesses, and he was permitted to present his own case.
The Court noted that there was no statutory rule or regulation that required the Vice-Chancellor to provide the appellant with a copy of the Inquiry Officer's report.
Crucially, the Court pointed out that the appellant never asked for a copy of the report. His grievance on this point was considered an "after thought."

Given that the appellant had a full opportunity to participate in the inquiry and defend himself, the Court found that the failure to proactively provide the report did not constitute a breach of natural justice in these specific circumstances.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the inquiry was fair and that the appellant had been given adequate opportunities for his defence. The Court held that there was no breach of the principles of natural justice, as the appellant was fully aware of the charges, participated in the proceedings, and never requested the inquiry report that he later claimed was essential for his defence.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court, in its jurisdiction under Article 226, is justified in interfering with the decisions of domestic tribunals appointed by educational bodies, such as universities, in cases of unfair means.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's action of filing a writ petition under Article 226 implies the argument that the High Court is justified and required to interfere with the university's decision, especially when alleging procedural flaws and violations of natural justice.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's position, upheld by the Division Bench and Supreme Court, is that the High Court should not interfere with the decisions of a domestic educational tribunal when the inquiry conducted was fair.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the principles of natural justice were violated because the appellant was not furnished with a copy of the inquiry officer's report before being called upon to give his explanation.
appellant_arguments: The impugned order was invalid because not providing a copy of the inquiry officer's report before the appellant was asked to submit his explanation was a breach of the principles of natural justice.
respondent_arguments: There was no breach of natural justice because the appellant was fully informed of the charge, participated in the inquiry, cross-examined witnesses, and presented evidence.
No statutory or other rule required the university to provide a copy of the report.
The appellant never requested a copy of the report.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the inquiry held against the appellant for adopting unfair means was fair and provided adequate opportunities for defence.
appellant_arguments: The inquiry was not proper because the rules required it to be conducted by an officer designated by the Principal of the college where the examination took place, and this procedure was not followed.
respondent_arguments: The inquiry was fair and provided adequate opportunity for defence as the appellant was informed of the charge, the inquiry was held in his presence after due notice, and he was allowed to cross-examine witnesses and adduce evidence in his defence.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The requirements of natural justice are not codified rules and whether they have been met in a given case depends on its specific facts and circumstances, the constitution of the tribunal, and the rules under which it functions. There is no universal principle of natural justice that mandates a disciplinary proceeding must consist of two separate inquiries or that a copy of an inquiry report must be provided with a show-cause notice, so long as the accused is informed of the charges and given a fair opportunity to be heard and defend themselves.
obiter: Courts should be slow to interfere with the decisions of domestic tribunals, like those of educational bodies, and should not import all the procedural considerations that govern criminal trials into such inquiries.

The decisions of domestic tribunals can be based on probabilities and circumstantial evidence, and a court's jurisdiction is limited to determining if the decision is supported by any evidence at all, not to re-evaluate the evidence as if in an appeal.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: In dealing with petitions under Article 226 against the decisions of educational institutions, the High Court's jurisdiction is limited and it should be slow to interfere. It is not sitting as a court of appeal. As long as the domestic inquiry conducted by the educational body is fair, provides the student with an adequate opportunity to defend themselves, follows the principles of natural justice, and is not based on no evidence at all (considering probabilities and circumstantial evidence), the court is not justified in interfering with the order.
legal_tests_applied: The test for judicial interference under Article 226 with a domestic tribunal's decision is whether the impugned order is supported by any evidence at all, including probabilities and circumstantial evidence. The High Court is not to act as an appellate body.

The test for whether the principles of natural justice have been met depends on the facts and circumstances of the case, the constitution of the tribunal, and its rules. It does not automatically require that every disciplinary proceeding consist of two inquiries or that a copy of an inquiry report be furnished with a show-cause notice, unless a specific rule requires it or it was requested and denied.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the argument that not providing a copy of the inquiry officer's report was a breach of natural justice, reasoning that the appellant was fully informed of the charge, participated in the inquiry, cross-examined witnesses, and was permitted to adduce evidence. Furthermore, no statutory or other rule required the university to provide the report, and the appellant never requested a copy.

The court dismissed the notion that every disciplinary proceeding must consist of two inquiries (one before and one after the show-cause notice), stating, 'Such is not the requirement of the principles of natural justice. Law may or may not prescribe such a course.'

The appellant's case for High Court interference failed because the Supreme Court found that the inquiry was fair, the appellant had an opportunity to make his defence, and no animus or mala fides were pleaded, thus the High Court was not justified in interfering with the university's order.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's decision was upheld because the inquiry was deemed fair. The court found that the appellant was informed of the charge, the inquiry was held in his presence after due notice, and he was allowed to cross-examine witnesses and present evidence in his defence.

The university's procedure was found to be compliant with natural justice because the principles are not embodied rules and, in this specific case, there was no rule requiring the provision of the inquiry report, nor did the appellant ask for it.

The respondent succeeded because the court affirmed the principle that courts should be slow to interfere with the decisions of domestic tribunals of educational bodies, which have the jurisdiction to decide questions of unfair means based on evidence, including probabilities and circumstantial evidence.
policy_considerations: Courts should be slow to interfere with the decisions of domestic tribunals appointed by educational bodies like universities, as these institutions must deal with the serious problem of unfair means, and it is normally within their jurisdiction to decide all relevant questions.
It would not be reasonable to import into inquiries held by domestic educational tribunals all the considerations that govern criminal trials in ordinary courts of law.

The rules of natural justice are not embodied rules. The question of whether the requirements of natural justice have been met must depend to a great extent on the facts and circumstances of the case, the constitution of the tribunal, and the rules under which it functions.
